prompt_topic: bioresorbable vascular scaffolds in percutaneous coronary intervention
raw_text:
The paradigm of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has evolved remarkably, from plain old balloon angioplasty to the establishment of metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) as the therapeutic gold standard. Despite their success, metallic DES introduce a permanent foreign body, which carries long-term risks such as neoatherosclerosis, late catch-up phenomenon, and permanent caging of the vessel, which impairs physiological vasomotion. The concept of "vascular restoration therapy" was introduced to address these limitations [1]. By providing temporary mechanical support during the critical healing phase and subsequently undergoing complete bioresorption, bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were designed to allow the vessel to regain its physiological vasomotion and undergo late luminal gain.

The first clinical application of a polymeric BVS dates back to the Igaki-Tamai scaffold [2]. Although this early polymer lacked drug-eluting capability, its long-term evaluation confirmed that complete scaffold degradation indeed allowed for vascular restoration [3]. This paved the way for the development of the everolimus-eluting poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA)-based Absorb BVS (Abbott Vascular). Early clinical feasibility was demonstrated in the ABSORB Cohort A study [4], which reported favorable performance up to two years [5]. This was followed by the ABSORB Cohort B study [6], which evaluated an updated scaffold design. The promise of these early trials led to intense global enthusiasm and anticipation of a major shift in PCI practice [7].

Subsequently, several large-scale clinical trials were launched to compare the Absorb BVS against the standard-of-care metallic everolimus-eluting stent. The ABSORB II randomized trial compared the BVS to metallic EES [8], and its three-year results raised early discussion on clinical endpoints [9]. Concurrently, the pivotal ABSORB III trial [10], alongside ABSORB China [11] and ABSORB Japan [12], demonstrated non-inferiority of the BVS to metallic EES regarding target lesion failure (TLF) at one year. These encouraging regulatory trials led to widespread adoption in real-world clinical practice, supported by registries such as GHOST-EU [13], ABSORB Barcelona [14], and dedicated investigations in patients presenting with acute myocardial infarction [15].

However, as longer-term data accumulated, a significant safety signal emerged. Systematic meta-analyses of the randomized trials revealed a significantly higher risk of scaffold thrombosis (ScT) and target vessel myocardial infarction (TVMI) with the Absorb BVS compared to modern metallic EES [16,17,18]. These concerns were starkly highlighted by the AIDA trial, which evaluated BVS in routine clinical practice and was prematurely halted due to a disproportionate and alarming rate of late and very late scaffold thrombosis [19].

Extensive mechanistic studies, including optical coherence tomography (OCT) analyses, were conducted to understand this setback [20]. Investigators identified that the thick struts of the Absorb BVS (150 µm) disrupted laminar blood flow, promoted platelet activation, and delayed endothelialization [21]. Suboptimal implantation techniques—such as under-expansion, incorrect vessel sizing, and poor lesion preparation—significantly contributed to early and late scaffold failure. To mitigate these risks, the "PSP" protocol (comprehensive Pre-dilatation, precise Sizing 1:1, and mandatory Post-dilatation with non-compliant balloons) was developed and standardized [22]. Implementation of the PSP technique in the ABSORB IV trial demonstrated a significant reduction in device-related adverse events during early follow-up [23]. Long-term five-year outcomes of the ABSORB III trial eventually showed that the risk of adverse clinical events plateaued once the scaffold was completely resorbed (beyond three years), proving the transient nature of the BVS-associated hazard [24]. Nonetheless, due to the high profile of safety concerns, clinical guidelines downgraded BVS to Class III (not recommended) for routine coronary interventions [25].

The commercial withdrawal of the first-generation Absorb BVS did not end interest in bioresorbable technology. Instead, it catalyzed a shift toward alternative materials and designs. Magnesium-based scaffolds emerged as a highly attractive option due to the mechanical strength and rapid resorption of absorbable metal [26]. The first-generation magnesium stent proved the safety of the concept [27]. This led to the development of the sirolimus-eluting Magmaris BVS (Biotronik), which was successfully evaluated in the BIOSOLVE-I [28], BIOSOLVE-II [29], and BIOSOLVE-III trials, demonstrating excellent safety profiles and low rates of ScT. Concurrently, other next-generation polymer platforms, such as the Fantom tyrosine polycarbonate-based scaffold [30], have integrated ultra-thin struts (<100 µm) and improved radiopacity to overcome the structural limitations of early PLLA-based devices.

In conclusion, the clinical journey of BVS has been a valuable lesson in interventional cardiology. While first-generation thick-strut devices suffered from elevated risks of scaffold thrombosis, next-generation scaffolds with thinner struts and optimized implantation techniques hold significant promise for reviving the dream of vascular restoration.
